Rubus rolfei (long sold as Rubus calycinoides) is a low, mat-forming evergreen groundcover from Taiwan with small, crinkled, maple-like leaves that bronze in cool weather, tiny white flowers, and sparse, dull orange-red raspberry-like fruit that is edible but mild and seedy rather than flavorful. It is grown primarily as a tough, fast-spreading ornamental groundcover for slopes, walls, and container edges rather than for fruit production, tolerating foot traffic, heat, and a range of light conditions from partial shade to full sun. Shear back hard in late winter if growth becomes leggy, and take tip cuttings in summer to propagate new plants.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; creeping blueberry is native to the southeastern coastal plain and needs consistently acidic soil, so avoid liming or planting near concrete foundations.

Vaccinium crassifolium is a trailing, mat-forming evergreen blueberry native to sandy pinelands and coastal areas of the Carolinas, with small, glossy, leathery leaves that take on bronze-red tones in cooler weather, pale pink urn-shaped flowers in spring, and small, sweet, edible blue-black berries in summer that both people and birds enjoy. It roots as it spreads to form a dense, low, evergreen carpet well suited to acidic-soil groundcover plantings, slopes, and the front of a native shrub border in Gulf South and coastal Southeast landscapes. Mulch with pine straw to maintain soil acidity and moisture, and avoid overhead irrigation with hard, alkaline water, which can gradually raise soil pH and reduce vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in cool, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; false violet is native to cool northern and montane forests and struggles in hot, dry, or heavy clay conditions further south.

Dalibarda repens is a diminutive, creeping woodland groundcover with rounded, violet-like, evergreen leaves and two kinds of small white flowers — showy open blooms that rarely set seed and inconspicuous self-pollinating blooms low on the plant that do — followed by small dry, raspberry-like fruit. It forms a low, dense mat in consistently cool, moist, acidic woodland soil and is best used as a specialty groundcover in a shaded rock garden or native plant collection rather than a large-scale planting, since it spreads slowly and resents disturbance. Keep the soil evenly moist with a leaf-litter mulch and avoid summer drought stress, which quickly causes the shallow-rooted mats to decline.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; redwood ivory spreads by rhizome to form an evergreen groundcover beneath the dry shade of conifers, much like its relative epimedium does under deciduous trees.

Vancouveria planipetala is a Pacific Northwest native in the barberry family, with wiry stems bearing glossy, leathery, three-parted leaflets and airy sprays of small white flowers with reflexed petals in late spring that give the plant its inside-out common name. It forms a slowly spreading, weed-suppressing evergreen carpet well suited to the dry shade beneath redwoods, firs, and other conifers where few groundcovers thrive, and once established tolerates considerable summer drought under a woodland canopy. Trim back tattered winter foliage in early spring before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in fall to propagate or renew vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; vanilla leaf is native to moist conifer forests of the Pacific Northwest and spreads by rhizome into a dense colony once its cultural needs for cool, consistent moisture are met.

Achlys triphylla forms a uniform, deciduous groundcover of distinctive three-lobed, fan-shaped leaves atop wiry stems, with slender spikes of tiny white flowers lacking petals rising above the foliage in late spring; the dried leaves release a sweet, vanilla-like fragrance, giving the plant its common name and traditional use as a natural air freshener and insect repellent by Pacific Northwest indigenous peoples. It makes an elegant, uniform textural carpet under conifers and other acid-loving shade plants such as rhododendron and huckleberry, though it needs consistently cool, moist soil and does not tolerate hot, dry summers or heavy clay. Once established in the right conditions it requires little care beyond an annual leaf-litter mulch to replicate its native forest floor.
